claims.text: The corrosion resistance of duplex stainless steels is primarily caused by formation of a thin passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film becomes enriched in chromium and molybdenum.
The passive oxide film is self-healing.
Chromium and molybdenum enrichment occurs preferentially on the FCC phase.
In duplex stainless steel, the FCC phase is more noble than the BCC phase.
The more noble FCC phase protects the less noble BCC phase and thereby limits pitting and overall metal dissolution.
Duplex stainless steel contains both FCC and BCC phases.
Chromium and molybdenum are typical alloying elements in the duplex stainless steel under study.
Chloride-containing aqueous solutions at 60–100 °C and moderate pH are representative of relevant chemical-processing and nuclear-coolant service conditions.
The phase-localized passive layer is predominantly composed of Cr2O3 and molybdenum oxides.
Local micro-galvanic coupling between FCC and BCC regions limits anodic dissolution of adjacent BCC regions.
Selective oxidation of chromium and molybdenum creates a compact protective barrier.
The compact passive barrier suppresses electron transfer and metal-ion diffusion.
Isolation of the substrate by the passive film slows localized and pitting corrosion.
Duplex stainless steel will exhibit a lower corrosion current density than 316L under identical conditions.
Duplex stainless steel will exhibit delayed pitting initiation relative to 316L.
Cr and Mo enrichment on FCC domains will correlate with improved passivation and corrosion resistance.
The proposed mechanism holds in mild to moderate, near-neutral aqueous environments where passive-film formation is thermodynamically favored.
Very low pH or high chloride concentrations can break down the passive film and diminish its protective effect.
Prior findings support phase-dependent nobility and micro-galvanic corrosion in duplex stainless steel.

contradictions.description: The FCC phase is identified as more noble and the BCC phase as less noble, yet their galvanic coupling is said to protect the BCC phase and limit its anodic dissolution. Coupling a noble cathodic phase to a less noble phase ordinarily makes the less noble phase the preferential anode; the cited duplex-steel evidence likewise associates the BCC fraction with susceptibility to galvanic corrosion.
